title: Obesity in Adults: Pharmacotherapy and Bariatric Referral Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult with overweight or obesity in primary care, an internal medicine clinic or the emergency department: classification, assessment for causes and complications, goals, lifestyle plan, when to add orlistat, liraglutide or metformin with doses and cautions, when to refer for bariatric surgery, pre-operative work-up, post-operative follow-up, supplements, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and recognition of early surgical complications. Based on the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) Obesity Control Program guideline, the Saudi Arabian Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (SASMBS) 2020-2021 guidelines and the 2016 Saudi Medical Journal obesity guideline. Children and adolescents, pregnancy and endoscopic balloon therapy are outside this topic. Medicine-pathway restructure on 2026-10-18: medicines regrouped into branches, steps and give-all vs choose-one options; no dose, source or clinical claim was re-checked.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.

Medicine list restructured into a branched decision pathway on 2026-10-18. Doses, routes, adjustments, monitoring, contraindications and sources are unchanged from authoring-standard-2026-10-18-saudi6-v1-live.
unverifiedSections: Semaglutide, tirzepatide, phentermine, naltrexone-bupropion and other newer anti-obesity medicines are not in the MOH obesity guideline or the SASMBS guidelines read; the MOH guideline lists semaglutide only as a weight-neutral diabetes medicine (Table 10). No dose or criteria for these are given here, and their SFDA status and local availability were not verified. A Saudi 2024 update of the obesity guideline exists (International Journal of Clinical Medicine) but could not be opened from this environment.

Neither the MOH guideline nor the 2016 guideline gives a numerical weight-loss target at 3 months for continuing orlistat or liraglutide; they say to evaluate efficacy after the first 3 months and continue if the loss is satisfactory.

The 2016 guideline suggests metformin (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence) but gives no dose; the dose shown is only the assumption used in its cost estimate (850 mg twice daily), not a recommended dose, and metformin for obesity is off-label.

The MOH guideline gives no renal or hepatic dose adjustment, older-adult dosing, maximum liraglutide step timing beyond the stated weekly 0.6 mg increases, or management of missed doses for orlistat or liraglutide; check the product monograph.

The Table 14 thiamine treatment line for Wernicke encephalopathy is partly illegible in the PDF image, so that dose is not quoted here; a clinician must check the printed table or local protocol. Serum albumin and ionised calcium units in Table 14 appear misprinted in the source and are not used.

The SASMBS document contains typographical and formatting errors (for example duplicated and broken numbering); its criteria are quoted as printed and the surgical indication wording differs slightly from the MOH guideline (SASMBS: BMI 40, or 35 with any comorbid factor; MOH: BMI 35 to 39.9 with a serious comorbidity and failure of initial weight-loss goals at 6 months).
Intragastric balloon therapy is mentioned only as a temporary measure (maximum 6 months, SASMBS) and is not detailed.
Bariatric procedure choice, operative technique and revision surgery are outside this topic; refer to the bariatric surgeon.

The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified. The MOH obesity guideline states that orlistat and liraglutide are SFDA-approved for obesity; check hospital formulary for local availability.

The MOH PDF and the SASMBS PDF were converted to text and key tables (pharmacotherapy, surgery indications, complications, supplements, laboratory appendix) were checked against page images; the 2016 guideline was read in text form. Figures should still be spot-checked against the source at clinical review.

Medicine pathway: branch entry criteria, preferred options and “use when” conditions were assigned from this topic's own indications and management steps. Confirm each against the cited guideline before clinical use.

pathophysiology.summary: Obesity is a chronic, relapsing disease of excess or dysfunctional adipose tissue with metabolic, mechanical and psychosocial effects; it raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, joint disease, fatty liver and reflux (SASMBS; MOH). Body mass index (BMI) classification for the Saudi (Middle-Eastern) population uses the same cut-offs as Caucasian populations: overweight 25.0 to 29.9, class I 30.0 to 34.9, class II 35.0 to 39.9, class III 40 or more kg/m2 (MOH Table 5). Waist circumference of 102 cm or more in men and 88 cm or more in women marks increased risk; BMI can overestimate fat in muscular people and underestimate it where muscle has been lost (MOH). Weight loss of 5 to 10% reduces cardiovascular and metabolic risk at BMI 25 to 35, while more than 15 to 20% is needed for sustained comorbidity improvement at BMI above 35 (MOH, citing SIGN). Many common medicines cause weight gain (some antipsychotics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, steroids, insulin, sulfonylureas, beta-blockers, progestins); stopping or substituting them is part of treatment (MOH Table 10; SASMBS).

symptoms: Excess weight gain over months to years; difficulty losing weight.
Snoring, daytime sleepiness or witnessed apnoeas (sleep apnoea).
Joint pain, reflux, low mood, binge or night eating.
Oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism or acne in women (polycystic ovary syndrome).
physicalSigns: BMI 25 or more; waist circumference 102 cm or more (men) or 88 cm or more (women).
Moon face, thin skin, easy bruising or striae suggest Cushing syndrome (MOH Appendix 5-7).
Neck circumference above 43 cm (men) or 41 cm (women) suggests sleep apnoea (MOH Appendix 5-7).
redFlags: After bariatric surgery: tachycardia, worsening abdominal pain, fever, raised white cell count or low urine output means anastomotic leak: urgent surgical referral (MOH Table 12).
After bariatric surgery: severe pain, swelling, tenderness and redness in a leg or arm means deep vein thrombosis: emergency referral; think pulmonary embolism (MOH Table 12).

After gastric bypass: unexplained intermittent abdominal pain with nausea or vomiting: internal hernia; plain films may be normal, so urgent computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and bariatric surgeon review to avoid small bowel gangrene (MOH Table 12).
Persistent vomiting or dysphagia after surgery: stenosis; confusion, ataxia or eye signs with vomiting: consider thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy (MOH Table 14).
Epigastric pain with possible bleeding or perforation: marginal ulcer; stop tobacco, aspirin and anti-inflammatory drugs (MOH Table 12).
Features of Cushing syndrome, severe hypothyroidism or eating disorder: screen before labelling simple obesity (MOH Appendix 5-7; SASMBS).
Pregnancy or planned conception: no obesity drugs; avoid pregnancy for 12 to 18 months before and after surgery (MOH; SASMBS).
precipitants: Poor sleep, stress, circadian disruption and late-night eating (SASMBS).
Family history, binge or night eating disorder, depression (MOH Appendix 5-3).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin; thyroid stimulating hormone raised; test only if suspected (MOH Appendix 5-7).

Moon face, thin skin that bruises easily, severe fatigue, striae; screen with a 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol (SASMBS; MOH Appendix 5-7).
Oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, palpable ovaries, acne, impaired glucose tolerance; androgens and pelvic ultrasound (MOH Appendix 5-7).
Hypersomnolence, right-sided heart failure signs, raised jugular venous pressure, leg oedema; blood gases and polysomnography (MOH Appendix 5-7).
Onset after a new antipsychotic, antidepressant, steroid, insulin, sulfonylurea or progestin; switch where possible (MOH Table 10).

clinicalManagement.title: First contact: classify and screen
actions: Measure height and weight, calculate BMI, and measure waist circumference when BMI is 25 to 35; classify using Saudi cut-offs (MOH).
Take a weight, nutrition, physical-activity, psychological, sleep, substance and medicine history (MOH Appendix 5-3); screen for depression, eating disorder and mood disorder.

Check blood pressure, heart rate, fasting glucose or haemoglobin A1c and lipid profile in everyone; add thyroid, Cushing, sleep apnoea or polycystic ovary tests only when suspected (MOH Appendix 5-7).
Review every medicine against Table 10 for weight gain and stop or switch where possible (MOH; SASMBS).
Assess readiness to change using the 5 As framework (MOH).

clinicalManagement.title: Goals and lifestyle plan
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Start at diagnosis, review every 3 months
actions: Set goals: BMI 25 to 35, 5 to 10% weight loss or 0.5 to 1 kg a week for 6 months; BMI above 35 with comorbidity, more than 15 to 20% (MOH Figure 2).
Nutrition: reduce energy intake by 500 to 1000 kcal a day; at least 5 servings of fruit and vegetables daily; avoid processed foods; eat earlier in the day (MOH Figure 2; SASMBS).
Activity: at least 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic exercise plus 1 to 3 resistance sessions a week (MOH Figure 2).
Add cognitive behavioural therapy: self-monitoring, goal setting, problem solving, stimulus control, relapse prevention (MOH Figure 2); address sleep and stress (SASMBS).

clinicalManagement.title: Add medicine
clinicalManagement.timeframe: If lifestyle alone has not met the goal (consider if less than 0.5 kg a week lost at 3 to 6 months)
actions: Eligible: BMI 30 or more, or BMI 27 or more with adiposity-related complications, together with nutrition, activity and psychological support (MOH; SASMBS).
Discuss benefits, limits, side effects and the temporary nature of the weight loss; treatment is for chronic use, not short courses (MOH; SASMBS).
Orlistat 120 mg capsule three times daily with each main fatty meal, or liraglutide 3 mg daily after weekly titration from 0.6 mg (MOH Table 9).
Metformin is a conditional, off-label suggestion for overweight or obesity, particularly with prediabetes or diabetes risk factors; no dose recommendation (2016 Saudi guideline, Recommendation 9).
Evaluate efficacy after 3 months; continue if weight loss is satisfactory; stop otherwise (MOH).
Do not use obesity medicines in pregnancy, breastfeeding or when trying to conceive (MOH).
Obesity pharmacotherapy is managed by or with an obesity medicine physician (SASMBS).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer for bariatric surgery
actions: MOH criteria: BMI 40 or more without comorbidity; BMI 35 to 39.9 with at least one serious comorbidity who failed initial goals at 6 months; BMI 30 to 34.9 with metabolic syndrome or diabetes uncontrolled on medical therapy.

SASMBS criteria: BMI 40, or 35 with one or more comorbid factors; or class I obesity (30 to 34.9) with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes despite optimal medical therapy; plus repeated failed non-surgical attempts and willingness to follow up for life.

Exclusions: active alcohol or drug abuse, uncontrolled psychiatric illness, pregnancy or pregnancy planned within 12 to 18 months, correctable cause of obesity, severe heart failure or unstable coronary disease, end-stage lung disease, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, active cancer, inability to commit to supplements and follow-up (SASMBS).

Pre-operative work-up: pre-bariatric blood panel, upper endoscopy, electrocardiogram and chest X-ray over 40, sleep apnoea screening, endocrine, psychological, nutritional assessment, pregnancy counselling, smoking cessation at least 6 weeks before surgery (SASMBS; MOH Appendix 5-7).
Mandatory pre-operative weight loss is not required (SASMBS).

clinicalManagement.title: After surgery: prophylaxis, supplements and follow-up
actions: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily before surgery if BMI is below 40, and 40 mg twice daily if BMI is 40 or more; after surgery unfractionated heparin 5000 units three times daily or enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily from 12 hours; extend enoxaparin 40 mg once daily for 10 to 15 days after discharge; continue mechanical measures (SASMBS).

Lifelong supplements in chewable form: 2 adult multivitamins with minerals (iron, folic acid, thiamine), calcium 1200 to 1500 mg elemental (carbonate after sleeve; citrate after bypass), vitamin D 3000 IU with a target of 25-hydroxy vitamin D above 30 ng/mL, iron 18 to 60 mg daily, vitamin B12 (SASMBS).
Discharge medicines: calcium, vitamin D3, ferrous sulphate, multivitamin, thiamine 100 mg daily and a proton pump inhibitor for 4 to 8 weeks (SASMBS).

Follow-up: 2 and 4 weeks after discharge, then at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 24 months; primary care continues for at least 2 years (MOH Page 30); laboratory tests at 3, 6 and 9 months for 2 years, then yearly (MOH Table 13).

Review diabetes, blood pressure, lipid and thyroid medicines: reduce or stop agents as weight falls; basal insulin reduced by 30 to 35% around surgery; stop sulfonylureas, meglitinides, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and thiazolidinediones before surgery and adjust insulin (SASMBS).
Avoid long-term anti-inflammatory drugs after gastric bypass (MOH).
Avoid pregnancy for at least 12 to 18 months after surgery (SASMBS).
Weight regain or less than 50% excess weight loss with no anatomical cause: consider obesity pharmacotherapy (SASMBS).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise complications
actions: Leak, deep vein thrombosis and internal hernia: urgent or emergency surgical referral (see red flags) (MOH Table 12).
Dumping syndrome: small, regular meals with protein and complex carbohydrate; acarbose in refractory cases; dietitian (MOH Table 12).
Marginal ulcer: stop tobacco, aspirin and anti-inflammatory drugs; proton pump inhibitor (MOH Table 12).
Gallstones: ursodeoxycholic acid 300 mg twice daily for 6 months to prevent them; cholecystectomy in selected patients (MOH Table 12).

Nutritional deficiency: treat per MOH Table 14 (for example B12 1000 to 2000 micrograms a day orally or 1000 micrograms a week intramuscularly; folic acid 1000 micrograms a day; vitamin D 1500 to 9100 IU a day adjusted to response).

regimens.indication: Overweight (BMI 27 or more with adiposity-related complications) or obesity (BMI 30 or more), with lifestyle measures
regimens.frequency: Three times daily with each main fatty meal
regimens.duration: Evaluate at 3 months; continue if weight loss is satisfactory; chronic use
adjustments: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding, cholestasis, liver failure, nephrolithiasis, acute kidney injury and chronic malabsorption syndrome (MOH Table 9).
Advise the patient to expect loose, oily stools and flatus, to avoid fatty meals and to consider fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (2016 Saudi guideline).
Renal, hepatic and older-adult dose adjustments are not stated in the sources read.
monitoring: Weight and BMI at 3 months; gastrointestinal effects; liver function and kidney function if symptoms; fat-soluble vitamin status (MOH Table 9; 2016 Saudi guideline).
contraindications: Pregnancy and breastfeeding; cholestasis; liver failure; nephrolithiasis; acute kidney injury; chronic malabsorption syndrome. Interactions: fat-soluble vitamins, oral anticoagulants, levothyroxine, ciclosporin, anticonvulsants (MOH Table 9).

regimens.indication: Overweight (BMI 27 or more with adiposity-related complications) or obesity (BMI 30 or more), with lifestyle measures; weight regain after bariatric surgery
regimens.dose: Start 0.6 mg daily for 1 week; increase the daily dose by 0.6 mg each week until the target of 3 mg (steps 0.6, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.0 mg)
regimens.duration: Evaluate at 3 months; continue if weight loss is satisfactory; chronic use
adjustments: Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding, personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, past pancreatitis and hypersensitivity (MOH Table 9).
Slowed gastric emptying may alter absorption of other medicines (MOH Table 9).
Hypoglycaemia risk mainly in patients with diabetes on hypoglycaemic medicines: review their doses (MOH Table 9).
Renal, hepatic and older-adult dose adjustments are not stated in the sources read.
monitoring: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, fatigue; rare cholelithiasis and pancreatitis; weight at 3 months (MOH Table 9).
contraindications: Pregnancy and breastfeeding; personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2; past pancreatitis; hypersensitivity to liraglutide (MOH Table 9).

102 cm or more in men; 88 cm or more in women; measure when BMI is 25 to 35 (MOH Page 10).
BMI 25 to 35: 5 to 10% of body weight or 0.5 to 1 kg a week for 6 months. BMI above 35 with comorbidity: more than 15 to 20% (MOH Figure 2, Page 16).
BMI 30 or more, or BMI 27 or more with adiposity-related complications, with lifestyle measures (MOH Page 24; SASMBS: BMI 27 or more with comorbidity, or 30 or more with or without comorbidity).

BMI 40 or more without comorbidity; BMI 35 to 39.9 with at least one serious comorbidity (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, limited quality of life) after failing initial goals at 6 months; BMI 30 to 34.9 with metabolic syndrome or diabetes uncontrolled on medical therapy (MOH Page 28).

BMI 40, or 35 with one or more comorbid factors; metabolic surgery can be considered for class I obesity (30 to 34.9) with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes despite optimal medical treatment; long or repeated failed non-surgical attempts; understands risks and follow-up (SASMBS Chapter 3).

teaching.scope: Adult with overweight or obesity in primary care, an internal medicine clinic or the emergency department: classification, assessment for causes and complications, goals, lifestyle plan, when to add orlistat, liraglutide or metformin with doses and cautions, when to refer for bariatric surgery, pre-operative work-up, post-operative follow-up, supplements, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and recognition of early surgical complications. Based on the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) Obesity Control Program guideline, the Saudi Arabian Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (SASMBS) 2020-2021 guidelines and the 2016 Saudi Medical Journal obesity guideline. Children and adolescents, pregnancy and endoscopic balloon therapy are outside this topic.
learningObjectives: Classify with Saudi BMI cut-offs and screen for secondary causes and complications.
Lifestyle first, then orlistat or liraglutide at the stated thresholds with a 3-month review.
Refer for surgery by BMI and comorbidity criteria and keep follow-up lifelong.
pitfalls: Missing a medicine that causes weight gain.
Giving obesity drugs in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Reading a normal plain film as excluding an internal hernia after bypass.
Stopping supplements or follow-up after surgery.
keyPoints: Pharmacotherapy: BMI 30 or more, or 27 or more with complications; orlistat 120 mg three times daily with fatty meals; liraglutide titrated 0.6 mg weekly to 3 mg.
Surgery: BMI 40, or 35 with comorbidity; 30 to 34.9 if diabetes is uncontrolled.
After surgery: lifelong supplements, labs at 3, 6 and 9 to 12 months, enoxaparin prophylaxis.

patientEducation: Obesity is a chronic disease; treatment is for the long term and weight regain is common after stopping.
Orlistat works best with a lower-fat diet; expect oily stools; take a multivitamin.

After surgery take supplements for life, attend every follow-up, avoid pregnancy for 12 to 18 months, and seek urgent care for severe abdominal pain, leg swelling, persistent vomiting or palpitations.
lifestyleAndDiet: Reduce energy by 500 to 1000 kcal a day; 5 daily servings of fruit and vegetables; avoid processed foods and sugar-sweetened drinks; eat earlier in the day.
At least 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity plus 1 to 3 resistance sessions; stop smoking at least 6 weeks before surgery.
mdtReferrals: Primary care or internal medicine physician; obesity medicine or endocrinology; bariatric surgeon; clinical dietitian; psychologist or psychiatrist; physiotherapist; clinical pharmacist; anaesthesiologist and cardiology or sleep medicine as needed.
dischargeCriteria: After bariatric surgery discharge when oral fluids are tolerated, pain is controlled, supplements and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis are prescribed, and follow-up at 1 week and 30 days is booked (SASMBS).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Weight and BMI every 3 months; assess response to medicine at 3 months; after surgery review at 1 week, 30 days, then every 3 months for 2 years with laboratory tests, then yearly for life.
